findings.name: billing
findings.root_cause: The billing container uses envFrom referencing ConfigMap "billing-config", which does not exist in the namespace, so kubelet fails with CreateContainerConfigError and the pod stays Pending forever.
findings.fix: Create the missing ConfigMap billing-config in namespace billing (or remove the envFrom reference from the billing Deployment if it is no longer needed).

diagnosis.summary: billing pod is stuck in Pending with CreateContainerConfigError because its container's envFrom references ConfigMap \"billing-config\", which does not exist in namespace billing. Only kube-root-ca.crt exists there. Fix: create billing-config or drop the envFrom reference from the billing Deployment.

findings.name: mailer
findings.root_cause: mailer crash-loops with 'nc: bad address smtp-relay' because its pod sets dnsPolicy None with a custom nameserver 10.96.0.99 that does not resolve the in-cluster name, so it can never reach the healthy smtp-relay Service (which has a ready endpoint).
findings.fix: Remove the custom dnsConfig (nameserver 10.96.0.99) from the mailer Deployment pod template and restore dnsPolicy ClusterFirst so 'smtp-relay' resolves via the cluster DNS.

diagnosis.summary: The relay is not down: smtp-relay pod is Running/Ready, listening on port 25, and the Service has one ready endpoint. The mailer pod fails to resolve 'smtp-relay' ('nc: bad address') because its pod spec overrides DNS with dnsPolicy=None and a bogus custom nameserver 10.96.0.99, so every connection attempt fails and the container exits 1 in a restart loop. Fix: restore default cluster DNS (remove dnsConfig / set dnsPolicy ClusterFirst) on the mailer Deployment."

findings.name: orders-api
findings.root_cause: orders-api pod crash-loops (exit 1) because the container logs 'FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set' — the Deployment defines no env, envFrom or config volume for DATABASE_URL, so the app cannot start and the orders page has no backend.
findings.fix: Add DATABASE_URL to the orders-api Deployment (env var or a Secret/ConfigMap via envFrom) pointing at its database, then restart the pods.

diagnosis.summary: orders/orders-api Deployment is down: its only pod crash-loops with exit code 1 after logging 'FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set'. The Deployment spec sets no env/envFrom/volume providing DATABASE_URL, so the app exits immediately on every start; 0/1 replicas ready, which takes the orders page down. Fix: supply DATABASE_URL in the Deployment spec.

findings.name: thumbnailer
findings.root_cause: The log-shipper sidecar cannot reach the upstream collector, so it buffers 4MiB log batches into the /buffer emptyDir forever; with only a 20Mi ephemeral-storage limit the pod exceeds it within minutes and gets evicted (Failed/Evicted), after which the Deployment replaces it and the cycle repeats.
findings.fix: Fix or remove the dependency on the unreachable log collector; until then raise/remove the log-shipper ephemeral-storage limit (and cap the buffer, e.g. rotate/trim /buffer) so buffered logs do not fill the pod's local storage.

diagnosis.summary: thumbnailer pods in media are repeatedly evicted because the log-shipper sidecar (upstream collector unreachable) keeps buffering 4MiB batches into an emptyDir bounded by a 20Mi ephemeral-storage limit; each pod fills it within minutes, is evicted as Failed/Evicted, and the Deployment recreates it — matching the 'disappearing and replaced every few minutes' report. Root cause object to change: Deployment/thumbnailer (sidecar config/limits); victims: the two evicted pods.

findings.name: stock-db
findings.root_cause: stock-db container loads an unbounded in-memory index (tail /dev/zero) under a 24Mi memory limit, so it is OOMKilled (exit 137) on every start; each death makes stock-db:5432 unreachable, which is why stock-api logs 'unreachable' and exits FATAL.
findings.fix: Raise the stock-db container memory request/limit well above 24Mi (or fix the runaway index load); the 24Mi cap is what triggers the repeated OOMKill and takes stock-db:5432 down.

diagnosis.summary: stock-api crash/restart is a downstream symptom. Root cause: the stock-db Deployment runs its container with only a 24Mi memory limit while its command performs an unbounded in-memory index load (tail /dev/zero), so the pod is OOMKilled (exit 137) and back-off-restarting (3 restarts, 0/1 ready). Every death drops stock-db:5432, and stock-api then fails its connection retries and exits FATAL. Fix belongs to stock-db: raise its memory limit (or stop the runaway allocation).

status namespace is healthy before the demo: 1 pod total with no problem pods (st), only Normal events (Scheduled/Pulled/Started) for status-page-7c589b76d-hz9xd, Deployment status-page is 1/1 ready, and Service status-page (80->80) has 1 ready endpoint matching the pod's container port. No warnings or misconfigurations found.

findings.name: frontend
findings.root_cause: Today's deploy set the frontend container image to nginx:1.299-alpine, a tag that does not exist in docker.io/library/nginx, so the kubelet fails to resolve and pull it (ErrImagePull/NotFound) and the pod stays Pending with ImagePullBackOff.
findings.fix: Set the frontend Deployment container image to an existing nginx tag (e.g. nginx:1.27-alpine or the previously working tag), then roll out.

diagnosis.summary: The storefront frontend never starts because today's deploy pinned the container image to nginx:1.299-alpine, which does not exist upstream; the kubelet gets ErrImagePull (NotFound resolving docker.io/library/nginx:1.299-alpine) and the single pod is stuck in ImagePullBackOff, leaving the Deployment 0/1 ready. Fix: point the Deployment at a real nginx tag.

findings.name: nightly-export
findings.root_cause: The export container exits 2 with "permission denied: cannot write /exports/orders-2026-09-27.csv"; the pod mounts no writable volume at /exports (only the service-account token), so every attempt fails and the Job hit its backoff limit, producing no file.
findings.fix: Give the job a writable destination for /exports: mount a PVC or emptyDir volume at /exports in the job's pod template (and ensure the container user can write it), then re-run the job.

diagnosis.summary: Last night's export produced no file because Job exports/nightly-export failed both attempts: the export container exited 2 with \"permission denied: cannot write /exports/orders-2026-09-27.csv\". The pod spec has no volume mounted at /exports (only the service-account token), so the write target is not writable/persistent. The Job reached BackoffLimitExceeded after 2 failures. Fix: add a writable volume (PVC or emptyDir) mounted at /exports in the job's pod template and rerun."

findings.name: accounts-api
findings.root_cause: accounts-api pod is stuck in Init:Running because init container wait-for-db loops on 'nc -z accounts-db 5432' → bad address; no Service named accounts-db exists (the DB service is actually named accounts-database), so DNS resolution of accounts-db never succeeds.
findings.fix: In the accounts-api Deployment, change the wait-for-db init container command to target the real service name accounts-database (or add a Service/alias named accounts-db); then the pod will initialize and start.

diagnosis.summary: accounts-api has been stuck starting because its init container wait-for-db cannot resolve the hostname it probes. The init command hardcodes 'nc -z accounts-db 5432', but the only database Service in the namespace is named accounts-database (healthy, 1 ready endpoint). No Service named accounts-db exists, so the init loop never completes and the main container never starts. Fix: point the init container at accounts-database (or create an accounts-db alias).

findings.name: ledger
findings.root_cause: The ledger container exits with code 2 at startup because its config value for key "retries" is the string "three" instead of an integer, so the pod crash-loops and the Deployment has 0 ready replicas.
findings.fix: Fix the ledger configuration: set retries to an integer (e.g. 3) in the config source feeding the ledger app, then restart the pod.

findings.name: ledger-api
findings.root_cause: Service ledger-api selects app=ledger-gateway but no pods carry that label (pods are labeled app=ledger and app=ledger-api), so it has 0 matching pods and 0 ready endpoints and does not answer.
findings.fix: Point the service selector at the real workload, e.g. change selector to app=ledger-api (or add the app=ledger-gateway label to the intended pods).

diagnosis.summary: Two independent faults in namespace ledger. (1) Deployment 'ledger' crash-loops: its container panics on startup with 'invalid config key \"retries\": expected integer, got \"three\"' and exits 2 (BackOff events, 0/1 ready). (2) Service 'ledger-api' has no endpoints: its selector app=ledger-gateway matches no pods (existing pods are labeled app=ledger / app=ledger-api), so it cannot answer even though the ledger-api deployment itself is 1/1 healthy."

findings.name: report-worker
findings.root_cause: Container is OOMKilled (exit 137) because its memory limit of 32Mi is too low for the workload's 'warming report cache' phase; it dies seconds after start, so no app error appears in logs and the pod crash-loops with BackOff.
findings.fix: Raise the container memory limit on the report-worker Deployment (e.g. from 32Mi to at least 128Mi, ideally based on observed peak usage) and restart the rollout.

diagnosis.summary: report-worker in namespace reports is not an app bug: the container is OOMKilled (exit code 137) within seconds of starting because its memory limit (32Mi, request 16Mi) is below what the 'warming report cache' workload needs. The kernel kills it before it can log anything, which explains the 'no error in logs' symptom. Fix: raise the memory limit on the report-worker Deployment.

findings.name: checkout
findings.root_cause: Service checkout selects app=checkout-v2, but the checkout Deployment labels its pods app=checkout, so the selector matches 0 pods and the Service has no ready endpoints — clients hitting the Service get connection refused even though the pod is healthy.
findings.fix: Align the label: either change the Service selector to app=checkout or relabel the checkout Deployment's pod template to app=checkout-v2 (and roll out).

diagnosis.summary: Checkout pods are healthy (1/1 ready, nginx running), but Service 'checkout' in namespace checkout uses selector app=checkout-v2 while the Deployment labels its pods app=checkout. The Service therefore has 0 matching pods and 0 ready endpoints, producing connection refused for callers. Root cause is the label mismatch; fix by aligning the Service selector with the pod labels (or vice versa)."

findings.name: cache
findings.root_cause: cache pods are Pending/Unschedulable because the Deployment's pod template carries nodeSelector disktype=nvme, while the only node doctor-lab-control-plane is labeled disktype=standard, so 0/1 nodes match.
findings.fix: Remove or correct the nodeSelector on the cache Deployment (change disktype=nvme to disktype=standard, or drop it) so the pod can be scheduled on the existing node; alternatively add an nvme-disk node and label it disktype=nvme.

diagnosis.summary: cache deployment never gets a running pod: its pod template requires nodeSelector disktype=nvme, but the single cluster node is labeled disktype=standard, so the scheduler reports 'didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector' and the pod stays Pending. Root cause is the Deployment spec; fix by correcting/removing the nodeSelector or adding a matching node.

findings.fix: Raise LimitRange 'defaults' default memory to fit statement-builder's real usage, or set explicit memory requests/limits (>=128Mi) on the Deployment container so the injected 32Mi default no longer applies.
findings.name: defaults
findings.root_cause: statement-builder sets no memory limit, but namespace LimitRange 'defaults' injects a 32Mi default memory limit; the workload loads ~50MB of ledger data, exceeds that limit, and is OOMKilled (exit 137), crash-looping.

diagnosis.summary: statement-builder is OOMKilled despite setting no memory limit because finance LimitRange 'defaults' injects a 32Mi default memory limit (16Mi request). The workload loads ~50MB of ledger rows, exceeds the injected limit, exits 137 and back-off-restarts. Root cause object: LimitRange 'defaults' (or add explicit memory limits to the Deployment).

findings.name: ml-trainer
findings.root_cause: ml-trainer requests 64 CPUs (cpu request "64") but the cluster's only node has just 2 allocatable CPUs, so the scheduler reports '1 Insufficient cpu' and the pod stays Pending; preemption is not helpful because no other pods could be evicted to free 62+ CPUs.
findings.fix: Lower the container CPU request in the ml-trainer Deployment to a value the node can satisfy (node allocates 2 CPUs total), e.g. cpu: 1 or less depending on real need.

diagnosis.summary: ml-trainer has been Pending because its pod requests 64 CPUs while the single node doctor-lab-control-plane only has 2 allocatable CPUs. Scheduler event: '0/1 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu'. Fix: reduce the CPU request in the ml-trainer Deployment spec."

findings.name: team-quota
findings.root_cause: renderer was scaled to 5 replicas but the namespace ResourceQuota team-quota caps pods at 2 (used: 2), so pod creation is rejected with 'exceeded quota: team-quota' and only 2 of 5 replicas can run.
findings.fix: Raise the pods limit in batch/team-quota (or add a separate quota) to at least 5 so renderer's desired replicas fit.

diagnosis.summary: renderer Deployment in batch wants 5 replicas but only 2 exist because ResourceQuota team-quota limits the namespace to 2 pods (already used). The deployment's ReplicaFailure condition shows FailedCreate: pods forbidden, exceeded quota. Fix is to raise the pods limit on team-quota; no pod-level fault exists (the 2 running pods are healthy).

findings.name: reporting-api
findings.root_cause: reporting-api requests 300m CPU / 256Mi memory but observed usage is ~0m CPU and 3Mi (p95); the request is idle, costing ~$7.69/month of wasted reservation
findings.fix: Lower reporting-api container requests to about 10m CPU and 8Mi memory (~1.5-2x the 0m/3Mi p95, above minimums)

diagnosis.summary: Rightsize audit of analytics: only reporting-api is materially over-provisioned — it requests 300m CPU / 256Mi while using ~0m CPU / 3Mi at p95, wasting ~$7.69/month; recommend 10m CPU / 8Mi. cache (10m/8Mi requested, $0.25/mo idle) is already small and not worth changing; ingest-worker is pinned at its 50m CPU limit 100% of the time (throttled), so it must NOT be cut — if anything it needs more headroom. No problem pods in the namespace.

findings.name: web
findings.root_cause: The web Deployment's readiness probe does HTTP GET on port 8081, but the nginx container runs with its default config listening on port 80; the probe gets connection refused, so the pod stays NotReady and the deployment shows 0/1 ready with no traffic.
findings.fix: Change the readiness probe in the web Deployment to target port 80 (nginx's actual listen port), or set nginx to listen on 8081 via config/env; then the pod will become Ready.

diagnosis.summary: web/web pod is Running but NotReady: readiness probe hits http://pod:8081/ and gets connection refused (25 events). The container is stock nginx (default config, listening on port 80) with no custom ports declared. Root cause is the Deployment's readiness probe pointing at the wrong port (8081 instead of 80). No Service exists in the namespace, but the immediate blocker for readiness is the probe mismatch.

findings.fix: Change the Service's targetPort from 8080 to 80 (the containerPort nginx actually listens on), then re-test calls to pricing-api:80.
findings.name: pricing-api
findings.root_cause: Service pricing-api forwards port 80 to targetPort 8080, but the pricing-api container listens on containerPort 80 (nginx); nothing listens on 8080 in the pod, so all calls through the Service are refused even though the pod is Ready.

diagnosis.summary: pricing-api pods are healthy and ready (1/1, endpoint registered) because their readiness probe hits port 80 directly. The Service, however, targets port 8080 while the nginx container only listens on containerPort 80 — no process on 8080, hence connection refused for every call via the Service. Fix is a one-line change of the Service targetPort to 80.

findings.name: search-web
findings.root_cause: Liveness probe execs a 300,000-iteration busy-loop before wget; with timeoutSeconds=1 it always times out, so kubelet SIGQUITs the healthy nginx (exit 0, no app errors) and the pod restarts every few minutes.

diagnosis.summary: search/search-web crash-loops with clean exit code 0 and no application errors because its own liveness probe is broken: the exec command starts with a 300,000-iteration busy-loop that cannot finish within timeoutSeconds=1, so the probe always times out and kubelet kills the healthy nginx container. Fix belongs in the Deployment's livenessProbe spec.
